title: Changing Social Hierarchies and Challenges to State Power
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: Transoceanic empires created new social hierarchies organized explicitly around race. The joining of the hemispheres threw together Europeans, Indigenous Americans, and Africans in colonial societies that had never existed before, and colonizers built rigid systems to rank and control these mixed populations.

In 1700s Spanish colonial Mexico, 'casta paintings' depicted combinations of European, Indigenous, and African ancestry, each labeled with a special name, mapping human worth by ancestry and skin color with people of pure Spanish descent at the top.

The casta system was an elaborate ranking of people in Spanish colonial society by their European, Indigenous, and African descent. Where a person fell in this hierarchy shaped their legal rights, job prospects, taxes, and social standing.

At the top of the casta system stood peninsulares (people born in Spain), just below them creoles or criollos (people of European descent born in the Americas). Below came mixed-ancestry groups, with Indigenous people and enslaved Africans at the bottom.

In the casta hierarchy, mestizos were people of mixed European and Indigenous descent, and mulattoes were people of mixed European and African descent. These mixed categories occupied the middle of colonial society between the European elite and the Indigenous and enslaved populations.

The casta system was a genuinely new kind of social order. Earlier societies had steep hierarchies, but tying status systematically to race and ancestry in a multi-continental colonial setting had not existed before the transoceanic encounter. Race as a structuring principle of society is largely an early-modern invention.

Creoles were often wealthy, educated, American-born landowners and merchants, yet they were ranked below the peninsulares and shut out of the highest offices, which Spain reserved for those born in the mother country. This bred deep creole resentment that later helped ignite the Latin American independence revolutions.

The new global trade produced new elites: merchants and others enriched by global commerce rose in wealth and influence, while some older elites declined. The social pyramid of 1750 had new occupants, new rules, and new tensions.

Enslaved Africans resisted the Atlantic slave system constantly. Some rose in open revolt and many escaped, showing that the enslaved were never passive victims but active agents resisting their bondage.

Maroon communities were independent settlements formed by escaped enslaved people in the mountains, jungles, and swamps of places like Brazil, Jamaica, and Suriname. They built free societies and sometimes fought off colonial armies for decades; the most famous, Palmares in Brazil, survived for most of a century.

The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 in New Mexico saw Indigenous peoples temporarily drive the Spanish out and reclaim their land and religion. It was one of the most successful Indigenous revolts in North American history.

Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba, in present-day Angola, skillfully fought and negotiated against Portuguese expansion and the slave trade for decades in the 1600s, an example of African resistance to European encroachment.

Resistance was not only against European empires. Cossack uprisings challenged Russian authority, and the Ottoman, Mughal, and Chinese land empires faced their own peasant revolts. Across the early-modern world, expanding state power and coercion was met by organized resistance from below.

Continuity and Change Over Time (CCOT) is the historical reasoning skill of analyzing what transformed and what persisted across a span of history. A strong CCOT analysis names both specific changes and specific continuities rather than only describing change.

A CCOT answer begins by establishing the situation at the start of the time span (the baseline). Before the transoceanic age (c. 1450), societies worldwide were already steeply hierarchical, with hereditary elites, patriarchy, and widespread coerced labor including slavery and serfdom.

Major social CHANGES from c. 1450 to 1750 included new race-based hierarchies like the casta system, a new American-born creole elite resentful of peninsulares, new merchant classes enriched by global trade, and Atlantic chattel slavery's uniquely racialized, hereditary bondage on an unprecedented scale.

Major social CONTINUITIES from c. 1450 to 1750 included steep and unequal hierarchy, elite domination of the masses, reliance on coerced labor as the engine of economies, and enduring patriarchy. Often a deep pattern persisted even as its surface form changed.

A strong CCOT thesis holds change and continuity together, ideally with a 'form changed / pattern continued' structure: from 1450 to 1750 the bases and forms of social hierarchy changed dramatically (new racial and creole categories) even as steep inequality, elite dominance, and coerced labor persisted.

The most common CCOT mistake is writing an answer that is all change and forgets continuity (or vice versa). Whenever a prompt says 'continuity and change,' you must write at least one strong, specific continuity, and avoid vague continuities like 'people still lived.'

By 1750 the Americas and Afro-Eurasia were bound into a single, unequal, interconnected global system: technology opened the oceans, the Columbian Exchange fused the hemispheres, maritime empires built the extractive economy, and new racial hierarchies and resistance shaped society. Yet agrarian economies, steep hierarchies, and the powerful Asian land empires still dominated, with Europe's full rise still to come in Units 5–6.
